newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden to increase index-linked bonds - Debt Office.
newsitem.headline: Sweden to increase index-linked bonds - Debt Office.

text.p: Sweden's National Debt Office said on Tuesday that lending through index-linked bonds would increase.
"In the future we see a continued expansion, albeit at a slower rate," Lars Horngren, the office's chief economist, told Reuters.
In 1996, index-linked bonds were Sweden's fastest growing debt instruments with total volume rising by 60 billion crowns to 74 billion, corresponding to five percent of the office's total lending.
"We expect halved growth in 1997, or roughly 30 billion crowns," Horngren said.
Demand has increased since the office started with on-tap issues instead of auctions and the National Debt Office is positive about index-linked bonds.

"The loans mean cost advantages for the government," Horngren said. "A nominal bond contains a compensation for inflation uncertainty, something you do not have to pay for in an issue of index-linked bonds."
But the construction of the loan also means that the government takes a larger risk as the investor is guaranteed a certain interest rate, irrespective of inflation.
The government thereby has an interest in keeping inflation low, an interest that is not valid for regular bonds as inflation in that case would chip away at the debt.
"Of course it would be more expensive for the government if it implements economic policies which make inflation rise," Horngren said.
"But this is not the main argument for index-linked bonds on the part of the National Debt Office. Our task is to minimise the government's lending costs."
An inquiry about government lending will be presented on April 22 and if it proposes an increase in index-linked bonds it would be in line with the National Debt Office's view.
"It would not be anything that changes our plans," Horngren said, adding that the rate at which index-linked bonds would be increased could be an issue.
